growth_story.headline: Kiribati's income per person is still 25.1 percent below its 1975 phosphate-era peak, though fishing fees and public spending have lifted growth since 2011.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Kiribati peaked in 1975, near the end of phosphate mining on Banaba, and in 2025 it was still 25.1 percent below that peak, about where it first was in 1974. It fell 26.4 percent in 1976 and drifted lower through the 1980s, and the phosphate deposits were gone by independence in 1979, taking the main export earner with them. Growth averaged 0.5 percent a year from 1990 to 2000 and -1.5 percent from 2001 to 2010, when spending ran ahead of revenue, the reserve fund built from phosphate money shrank per person, and the global crisis and high food and fuel prices brought contractions in 2009 and 2010. Since 2011 growth has averaged 3.2 percent a year, helped first by a regional scheme that raised the fees foreign fleets pay to fish from 2012 and by donor-funded airport and seaport works. More recently growth has rested mostly on public spending, including higher public wages, while the sources describe private production as subdued. Growth averaged 2.6 percent a year over 2016 to 2025, up from 1.9 over 2006 to 2015.

threads.title: Phosphate runs out
threads.text: Phosphate mining on Banaba was the country's main export earner until the deposits ran out by independence in 1979. The money was partly saved in a reserve fund, but output has long struggled to keep up with a growing population, so income per person has stayed flat for decades.

threads.title: A lost decade of deficits
threads.text: In the 2000s government revenue fell behind spending, and the gap was filled by drawing down the phosphate reserve fund and by costly borrowing. High food and fuel prices and the global crisis then brought contractions in 2009 and 2010; inflation reached 13.7 percent in 2008.

threads.title: Fishing fees reset in 2012
threads.text: From 2012 a regional scheme that sells fishing days to foreign fleets sharply raised what Kiribati earns from its tuna waters. Together with donor-funded airport and seaport works, it supported steady growth from 2011. Income per person grew 9.8 percent in 2015, a year when investment reached 38.6 percent of GDP.

threads.title: Fishing rents fund the state
threads.text: The government still lives mainly on fishing fees, grants and withdrawals from the reserve fund, and spends close to the size of the whole economy. A trend decline in fishing revenue, together with higher spending, has weakened the budget and the external accounts compared with before COVID.

threads.title: Public pay drives recent growth
threads.text: Growth since COVID has leaned on the public sector, including a large public pay rise in 2024 that lifted household spending. Higher wages and subsidies have widened the budget deficit, which is paid for from cash reserves and the reserve fund.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 2.7 percent in 2025, after 3.1 percent in 2024, and inflation rose to 6.5 percent in 2025 as regulated fuel and power prices were raised. In May 2026 the IMF said Kiribati's recent growth had outpaced other Pacific islands and poverty had fallen, but that inflation was under renewed pressure from higher fuel and shipping costs caused by the war in the Middle East. In October 2026 the World Bank expected growth to ease in 2026, with a wider deficit as the government absorbs part of higher oil prices.

growth_story.tension: The ADB describes four straight years of economic growth in 2001 to 2004, yet in the data income per person fell in every year from 2001 to 2005, because output did not keep up with a growing population. In the same way, the IMF said in 2025 that the economy was close to its pre-COVID trend, while income per person in 2025 was still 25.1 percent below its 1975 peak.
